33_interl17: modestly, of himself as if of another
33_marg8: The vision of Isaias, etc. There are three kinds of vision. The first is bodily, by which we see heaven and earth and the like. The second is spiritual, by which we see, as in every image, the likeness of men and the like. The third is intellectual, which is in reason, by which we know the Creator, and by the revealing of the Holy Spirit understand whatever it may be. To see also is often put for to understand. Whence we often ask, saying, “Do you see?” that is, “Do you understand?” The prophets also are hence called seers, that is, those who understand. This vision Isaias saw; the Holy Spirit, namely, inspiring him, he understood what was to come. Whence in the beginning he does not set down visions as Daniel does, nor does he say what he saw, but at once says: “Hear, O ye heavens,” and “give ear.”
33_marg9: Not only Isaias but also the others who have in the title “the vision which this one or that one saw” do not bring in what they saw, for example, “I saw the Lord sitting,” but at once relate what was said, as here: “Hear, O ye heavens,” etc. And: “Thus saith the Lord to Idumea.” For the prophets are rightly called seers, whose eyes are always on the Lord, according to that: “To thee have I lifted up my eyes, who dwellest in heaven,” and elsewhere: “Lift up your eyes, and see the countries, for they are white already,” etc. Of these eyes it is said: “The light of thy body is thy eye.” And the people saw the voices, that is, understood. So those who saw thus were not, as Montanus would have it, without understanding.
33_marg10: Isaias means saviour of the Lord; Juda, confession; Jerusalem, vision of peace; Ozias, strength of the Lord; Joathan, perfection of the Lord; Achaz, holding or strong; Ezechias, rule of the Lord. For he who is saved with the Lord presiding, and is the son of Amos, that is, of the strong and robust, perceives spiritually the vision of confession while he mourns his former sins, and of peace when after penance he passes over to the light and rests in eternal peace; and all his times pass under the strength of the Lord, and in perfection and robustness. And when he has done all things, he says: I am an unprofitable servant; I have done that which I ought to do.
33_marg11: Amos, the father of Isaias, is not the third of the twelve prophets; for among the Hebrews they are written with different letters. This one has as first and last letters aleph and sade; the other, ain and samech. And this one, they say, is interpreted strength or robust; the other, a heavy or hard people. But this one was a prophet, if we agree with the Hebrews, who maintain that the fathers, grandfathers and great-grandfathers of the prophets, whose names are set down at the beginning of their prophecy, were prophets.
33_marg12: Isaias speaks principally of the two tribes, that is, Juda and Benjamin, with the exception of the ten which are called Israel and Ephraim, which Phul, king of the Assyrians, had already begun to lay waste under Ozias, king of Juda. Finally, in the fifty-second year of his reign, while Phacee the son of Romelia was reigning in Samaria, Theglathphalasar, king of the Assyrians, took, with many others, Galilee and all the land of Nephtali, and carried them over to the Assyrians. From this it is shown that these things were foretold, with the overthrow of Samaria near at hand, for the correction of the two tribes.
33_marg13: The vision of Isaias, etc. For Juda, in which the two tribes are signified, the Septuagint and Theodotion put Judea, which signifies the whole land of the twelve tribes. And where we translate from the Hebrew “concerning Juda and Jerusalem,” they put “against Judea and Jerusalem.” Symmachus more plainly: “of Juda and Jerusalem”; he wishes neither prosperity nor adversity to be shown in the title, but only that the prophet foretold concerning Juda and Jerusalem.
33_marg14: I know that some interpret Juda and Jerusalem as heavenly things, and that Isaias puts forward the person of the Lord, who foretells their captivity in our land and their return to the holy mount in the last days. We, judging these things contrary to the faith, despise them all, and following the truth of the history, whatever they dream about the heavenly Jerusalem, we refer to the Church of Christ and to those who either leave her because of sin or return through penance; of which it is said: “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem: for thy light is come,” etc.
33_interl30: of the strength of the Lord
33_interl31: of the perfection of the Lord
33_interl33: of the rule of the Lord
33_marg15: Ozias is the same who is also Azarias. It is easy to know, from the kings who are set down in the title, that Isaias, Osee, Joel and Amos prophesied at one and the same time. But the beginning of the word of the Lord was in Osee. As for what is said in the title, that he prophesied under Ozias, Joathan, Achaz and Ezechias, unlike the other prophets we do not know what was said specially under each one, because it is fully distinguished up to the end of the volume.
33_marg16: It should also be known that Ezechias began to reign in Jerusalem in the twelfth year of Romulus (who founded a city in Italy named after himself), so that our histories appear older than the Gentile ones.
33_interl39: metonymy, the container for the contained: heaven, that is, the heavenly ones; earth, the inhabitants of the earth
33_marg17: Hear, O ye heavens, etc. Above, it has been shown in the title who the prophet is, whose son, what he saw against Juda and Jerusalem, and in what time. Now he calls heaven and earth to hear. For the Lord, through Moses, calls heaven and earth when he gave his law to the people of Israel: “Hear, O ye heavens, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.” After the people’s transgression he calls the same as witnesses, that all the elements may know that God is justly roused to anger in vengeance for his commandments. He wished, moreover, heavens to be said in the plural and understood in the singular, as we say or call single cities Thebes or Athens.
33_marg18: Samayn in Hebrew signifies the heavens in the plural; so all words that end in a syllable are masculine and plural, as cherubim and seraphim; those in oth are feminine plurals, as Sabaoth. Hear, O ye heavens, etc. Things that are lofty have the greater understanding, those lower an earthly one. Whence: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” Let him therefore who is heavenly hear the allegory; let him who is earthly hear the history.
33_marg19: Some think heaven and earth are summoned to hear as if they were living things, in accord with that: “He looketh upon the earth, and maketh it tremble”; since this power is of God, and is not to be understood in an earthly way.
33_interl40: not to you who are unworthy, but to me
33_marg20: Not to you but to me, so that I may report to you what I heard in the spirit, you who do not deserve to hear it yourselves.
33_interl42: the Jews, whom he deigns to call sons
33_interl43: I have brought up, not begotten, according to some, as some codices have it; for whosoever is born of God sinneth not
33_interl46: by casting off my precepts and despising the prophets
33_interl47: who did such great things for them
33_marg21: I have brought up children, etc. As if: I adopted them as sons and called them firstborn, yet they were not won by benefits, even as brute animals are, so as to understand their nourisher. Nor does he compare them to the dog, a most keen animal, which for a little food defends the houses of its masters, but to the dull sense of the ox and the ass, of which one turns up the earth, the other carries men. Whence they are also called beasts of burden, because they help men.
33_marg22: I have brought up children, and, etc. From this place he relates what the Lord spoke to the children of Israel, whom he established as servants by the common law, but turned into sons, saying: “Israel is my son, my firstborn.” It is also said to the apostles that if they do the will of the Lord they shall not be called servants but friends. Israel is called firstborn lest he be proud, because there are also second sons from the Gentiles, and yet according to the mysteries of the Scriptures they do not receive the inheritance of the firstborn but of the second. Not Cain’s gifts but Abel’s were pleasing to the Lord. Nor did Ismael but Isaac receive the inheritance. Nor did Esau the firstborn but Jacob seize the blessing. Ruben also being set aside, the blessing of the seed of Christ is transferred to Juda. The Jews therefore, according to the order of the calling, were the first and the head called. We, the second and the tail, he says, have been turned into the head, and are called sons of God; whence: “He gave them power to be made the sons of God.”
33_interl49: those of the Jews who believed
33_marg23: The ox knoweth, etc. “Thou shalt not plough with an ox and an ass together,” as Ebion does, who confounds the Gospel and the Old Testament. Blessed is he that soweth upon all waters, where the ox and the ass tread, that is, in the divine sayings, namely of the holy Scriptures, of the old namely and new testament, and treads the water of the killing letter that he may reap the fruit of the life-giving spirit. The ox is referred to Israel, who bore the yoke of the law as a clean animal. The ass signifies the Gentile people, burdened with the weight of sins, to whom it is said: “Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened.”
33_marg24: A Gentile, or a convert, once wanton and unclean, burdened with sins, who believed in the incarnation of Christ, who, born, was at once laid in the manger, so that he might refresh all by the bridle of his flesh.
33_marg25: Scribes and Pharisees, having the key of knowledge and of the law. Whence those who saw God were called Israel.
33_interl55: Eternal damnation threatens eternal destruction, because they are unwilling to believe in the coming of the Son of God, who is to redeem the world
33_interl58: You are of your father the devil, and offspring of vipers; who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come?
33_marg26: Woe to the nation, etc. In the title he recalls the person, the cause and the time. Second, he makes them attentive. Third, he relates what the Lord has said. Fourth, as if in excess, he rebukes the sinful nation.
33_marg27: Woe to the nation, etc. He threatens eternal destruction because they reject the Son who brought salvation.
33_marg28: “Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead.” Whence elsewhere: “They are heavy upon me as a heavy burden.”
33_interl59: to the Jews who were first sons of God by benefit, and sons of iniquity by their own vice
33_interl61: worshipping idols, not receiving the Son of God
33_marg29: Others: the vice of the worst men, not of the seed, but of the malice of those who by their own will have forsaken God. For the nature of good and bad is not to be thought diverse.
33_interl62: worshipping idols, not receiving the Son of God
33_marg30: Others: the vice of the worst men, not of the seed, but of the malice of those who by their own will have forsaken God. For the nature of good and bad is not to be thought diverse.
33_interl63: no one putting his hand to the plough and looking back
33_marg31: Those who were called a part and sons of God, it is said of them: “The children that are strangers have lied to me.” No one putting his hand to the plough, etc. Whence the Apostle: stretching forth himself to those things which are before, forgetting those that are behind.
33_marg32: Why shall I strike you any more, etc. As if I had struck you in vain, since you did not receive correction; therefore my zeal will depart from you. Like that: “There is no soundness in their wound.”
33_marg33: God often strikes that he may correct. But to those who are incorrigible he says: “For what shall I strike you?” as if to say: I find no medicine that I may apply to you; all your members are full of wounds; I have applied healing often; now I find no part of the body that is not already struck and full of wounds. Or: I find no strokes by which to break your hardness; for the hardness grows the more as I apply greater scourges. That there is now no place fit for medicine he shows thus: the whole head is sick.
33_interl71: the wise, because wisdom is in the heart through affection; these, because they understand and lament both their own sins and those of others
33_marg34: The whole head is sick, etc. As gladness of soul sometimes lessens the pains of the body, and if languor of mind is added the infirmity is doubled; and as, if the head aches, all the members are weak; so, if the princes and teachers had kept justice, the people would somehow have had medicine. But because all have been made sick, the medicine of souls is taken away; whence: from the sole of the foot, etc.
33_interl72: from the least to the greatest
33_interl73: in the people, or in the head, or in the body
33_interl74: of mind, because they killed the physician
33_interl80: of penance, so that their hardness might be softened by the tears of compunction
33_interl81: The Septuagint: there is no plaster to apply, neither oil nor bandages.
33_marg35: Wound and bruise, etc. As if bodies either gape with wounds, or are black and blue from blows, or swell with stripes. This properly suits the final captivity, for which there is no remedy, and in which it is fulfilled: “All have gone aside, they are become unprofitable together.”
33_marg36: Wound: by a staff; bruise: by rods; stripe: by a sword; usually by a staff.
33_marg37: It should be known that these things were foretold of the Lord’s coming and of the last captivity, when they had by then received no cure, because they killed the true and merciful physician sent to them.
33_marg38: Whence: “We would have cured Babylon, but she is not healed”; the city, that is, of confusion and vices. We read also of the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, wounded by robbers, cured by the Samaritan, and after the sharpness of the wine, the softness of oil poured in. And it must be noted that from where he said: “For what shall I strike you,” etc., up to here, “nor dressed, nor fomented with oil,” he kept the figure and expressed the irremediable captivity of the Jews.
33_interl84: of the Babylonians or the Romans
33_marg39: Your land is desolate, etc. These things were partly fulfilled under the Babylonians, when the cities of Jerusalem were burnt and the region of the Jews overthrown; with the Samaritans dwelling there, and lions also laying waste the land; but wholly under the Romans.
33_marg40: Almighty God forsook Jerusalem, and the temple, and the people, whose guardian he himself was, while they bore the fruits of good works. Whence: “Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it.”
33_marg41: Allegorically. Those who have fallen from their former health and been handed over to hostile powers, all their goods come into desolation, and God will not remember their former justice, and all things will be set on fire by the fire of the devil and become food for beasts, of whom it is said: “Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee.”
33_marg42: Whence: “Arise, let us go hence”; and: “Your house shall be left to you desolate”; and elsewhere: “I have forsaken my house,” etc.
33_interl89: a vineyard stripped of its grapes, from which you carried the vine out of Egypt
33_interl90: which, the fruit having been taken away, the keepers left empty
33_marg43: The daughter of Sion, etc. By the affection of a most loving father, all are by nature sons, and by fault strangers. Whence Babylon is often called a daughter.
33_marg44: Morally. By Sion, which means watching, and which is called a paradise of fruits, and a vineyard, the soul is understood, which ought to stand in contemplation and bring forth acceptable fruits; and if the mind, that is the nous, presides over it, it has God as the guardian of the mind. But if vices and sins, like little beasts, have eaten up the shoots of the virtues, it immediately loses God as its guardian.
33_marg45: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” Therefore, after the boar out of the wood has laid it waste, and those passing by the way have gathered its grapes, it is left by the Lord.
33_marg46: Lord Sabaoth, which the Septuagint, according to the quality of the places, translate either Lord of powers or Lord almighty. For Christ, to whom it is said: “All power is given to me in heaven and in earth,” as he is God of God and Lord of Lord, so is he almighty Son of the Almighty.
33_interl94: Christ, of whom the Lord of hosts is himself the King of glory
33_interl95: the remnant of Israel will be made safe
33_interl97: the apostles and their followers; whence others
33_marg47: That is, in the apostles the remnant of the Jewish people was made safe, and on one day three thousand and five believed, and the gospel is spread abroad through the whole world.
33_interl99: dumb, from the praise of God. For Sodom is interpreted dumb, Gomorrha rough
33_interl100: rough through the enormity of sins
33_marg48: Except the Lord of hosts, etc. This is spoken in the person of the prophet and of the faithful from the same people.
33_marg49: Except the Lord, etc. Here it is shown that what was said against Juda and Jerusalem is to be referred to the captivity by the Romans, when in the apostles the remnant of the Jews were saved, and in one day three thousand believed, and the Gospel was sown in the whole world.
33_interl103: as you who boast yourselves to be sons of Abraham
33_interl104: to whom your father is like, the Amorrhite, and your mother the Cethite
33_interl105: with the outward ears at least
33_interl106: “You are of your father the devil.”
33_marg50: The remnant of the people of Israel having been saved through the apostles, the prophet, speaking likewise, turns to the scribes and Pharisees and the people crying out: “Crucify him, crucify him,” and calls them princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrha, who devised the worst counsel and bound the just one, and said: “We have no king but Caesar.”
33_marg51: The Hebrews say that Isaias was put to death for two reasons: that he called them princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrha, and that, when the Lord said to Moses: “Thou canst not see my face,” he dared to say: “We saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and elevated,” not considering that the seraphim covered the face and the feet of God, or their own, which is read ambiguously in the Hebrew, and that Isaias writes that he saw only the middle parts.
33_marg52: The remnant being saved through the apostles, the word is turned to the scribes and Pharisees and to the people crying out, “Crucify him, crucify him.”
33_marg53: Hear, etc. This pertains specially to the Jews of that time, to the scribes and Pharisees and to the people crying: crucify him, crucify him. For as the Sodomites sinned publicly, devising the worst counsel against the just man Lot, and without shame said: bring out the men that came in to thee, that we may abuse them; so these shamelessly said against Christ: come, let us devise devices against the just one; and he is guilty of death; and the like. Whence in what follows: “They have proclaimed their sin as Sodom, and they hide it not.”
33_marg54: Hear the word of the Lord, etc. The Hebrews hand down that Isaias was put to death because he had said this, or because he had said: “I saw the Lord,” etc. Whereas the Lord said to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live,” and “Thou canst not see my face”; nor do they consider the face or the feet of the Lord, or their own. For in the Hebrew it is said ambiguously: the seraphim covered, and Isaias wrote that he saw only his middle parts. Yet the angels, even of the lesser ones in the Church, always see the face of God, but man cannot. “For we see now through a glass in a dark manner,” etc. But when we advance from men into angels, we behold the glory of God with face revealed, although according to the property of nature no creature can see the face of God; and he is now discerned by the mind when he is believed invisible.
33_interl108: as if to say: since you do not keep the law, why do you offer?
33_marg55: As if you think I need these or delight in them. But I am full, that is, I need nothing. For “the earth is mine, and the fulness thereof.” Or, I am full, that is, filled with loathing, because you do not offer rightly.
33_marg56: “The holocausts of rams,” etc., down to: “Judge for the fatherless,” etc. He rejects the sacrifices of the Jews and commends the obedience of the gospel.
33_marg57: Burnt offerings of rams, etc. It points to the last destruction of the temple, which lasts forever. For after the Babylonian captivity the temple was built by Zorobabel, and sacrifice was offered in it for a long time.
33_marg58: It can also be understood of those who, despising God’s commands, wish to appease him by a multitude of sacrifices and to buy licence to sin. Or of those who offer robbery and greed upon the altar and bestow them on the poor.
33_marg59: Using the past tense, he shows that he never loved the sacrifices of the Jews, but endured them for a time because of what they signified, and once the true sacrifice was accomplished, counted them as nothing.
33_interl112: as if it were a spiritual law
33_marg60: God did not require these sacrifices as though he had need of them, but so that they would not sacrifice to demons, and so that through fleshly and typical things they might more easily come to the spiritual and true sacrifice.
33_marg61: Let the Ebionites hear this, who think the law must be kept after Christ’s passion. Let their associates hear this, who decree that it is to be kept only by the Israelite race.
33_interl120: I will no longer endure, because your assemblies are wicked
33_marg62: The feast of the new moon, which they celebrated at the beginning of the months. Neos, new; mene, moon. Whence: “Blow the trumpet in the new moon to the Lord.”
33_marg63: Because they do not offer spiritual sacrifices. Whence: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.”
33_marg64: Anthropopathism: not that he has a soul, but he speaks in our manner, as if: I have utterly hated.
33_marg65: Symmachus. I grew weary of pitying, as if I could no longer have mercy, because after the servants you killed the Son. As in Osee: “Destruction is thy own, O Israel: thy help is only in me.” Perish, Israel, who are saved not by your own merit but by my help alone.
33_interl127: which they did, as if imitating Moses, who prayed against Amalec with hands raised
33_interl133: From sin. Whence: “Deliver me from blood, O God, thou God of my salvation”, that is, from sins.
33_marg66: Of the prophets, at last, of their Lord. Whence: “Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers.” They slew the prophets; you slew the son of the householder.
33_marg67: This testimony is to be used against those who, having bloody hands from their daily deeds, keep watch in prayer day and night.
33_interl135: bring forth worthy fruits of penance
33_marg68: As if: the truth of the gospel pleases what I hated. Wash yourselves: with the blood of Christ, in the water of baptism. Be clean: afterwards, remaining in innocence of life. For baptism alone can be for the remission of sin; whence: “Unless a man be born again,” etc. And elsewhere: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father,” etc.
33_marg69: The order is chief: “wash yourselves” is not enough unless “be clean” is added, that after the washing of water they may have purity of heart. For “blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.” But having purity of heart, they must take away evil from their minds, not only in the sight of men but also in the sight of God, from whom nothing can be hidden. But what is added, “Cease to do perversely,” the gospel echoes: “Behold thou art made whole: sin no more.” Therefore, departing from vices, let him learn to do good, seek judgment, help the oppressed, defend the fatherless and the widow. But if he does these things, the sins that before were scarlet like blood will be forgiven, and the works of blood will be changed in the garment of the Lord, which is made of the fleece of the lamb, whom those follow in the Apocalypse who shine with the whiteness of virginity.
33_interl138: take away evils; in this way wash yourselves
33_interl140: if you at least think them, do not complete them
33_interl143: because it is an abomination to me
33_marg70: Virtue is to be learned and imitated, not trusting in nature; whence Jesus the son of Sirach: “If thou desire wisdom, keep justice, and God will give her to thee.” And Isaias: “Everyone who has not learned justice upon earth will not do truth.” Justice, therefore, is to be learned, and the thresholds of teachers are to be worn.
33_interl148: from the wise, whose office it is to judge; whence Solomon asked for wisdom to judge the people
33_interl150: that is, help him in judgment if his cause is good, because it is said: “Spare not the poor man in judgment”
33_interl151: that is, to the poor man
33_marg71: The evangelical commands succeed the sacrifices of the Jews. Provision is made for orphans and widows, so that, secure concerning their spouses and children, martyrs may go forth to war.
33_interl154: when you have done these good things
33_interl158: as if you had done these
33_interl159: Whence: “Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, O Lord”; and elsewhere: “his raiment white as snow”
33_marg72: The same is coccus and coccinum and vermiculus: a great sin, namely such as murder and adultery, etc. But that which is signified by the snow, and likewise by the wool, is the cleansing, namely the washing away of sins.
33_marg73: As snow, because they will be cold against the incentives of vices. And as wool, because they will be clothed against the cold of unbelief.
33_marg74: From which the garment of Christ is made; whence: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.” And elsewhere: “As I live, saith the Lord, thou shalt be clothed with all these as with an ornament.”
33_interl161: as if it lies in your own will
33_interl163: of the living, or of the present; so that at least the Jews, invited by present things, may obey
33_marg75: If you be willing, etc. Free will is reserved, so that it may be shown that rewards or punishments follow not from God’s prejudgment but from the merits of individuals.
33_marg76: Since the other elements are in motion, the earth stands immovable. Therefore by it is signified the firmness of eternal blessedness.
33_interl166: as if you should not doubt the truth
33_marg77: Of the Babylonians, or of the Romans, or of God: pestilence, namely death, famine, eternal punishment; for whatever afflicts is customarily called a sword.
33_interl167: The Word of the Father, or the prophet through whom God speaks his secrets, whose judgment is not changed while sins remain.
33_interl169: not so much by deed as by mind, by withdrawing from God
33_marg78: The Septuagint added Sion, for the sake of a clearer sense. Sion is the mountain on which Jerusalem was founded. But after it was taken by David it was called the city of David, in which there were holy men while it had the tabernacle of the Lord; and afterwards the temple, when Nathan and others prophesied, and Asaph and Idithun and Haneman and the sons of Core were set over the choirs, so that religion might pass little by little from the sacrifices of victims to the praise of God.
33_marg79: Justice in Hebrew is sedech, which signifies rather just, so that we understand the Lord dwelling in it, concerning whom; but what did the just man do? This is signified in Ezechiel by Oolibah, which is interpreted tabernacle, or my tabernacle in her.
33_interl173: because they killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets
33_marg80: How, etc. These things refer to the time of the prophet, but especially to the incarnation of Christ, when they wholly withdrew from God, choosing Barabbas and killing the Son of God; whence, wondering, he says: How, etc.
33_marg81: The faithful soul, full of judgment, while it obeys God, has God dwelling in it, who is justifying justice. But if it withdraws from God, it is inhabited not by place but by merit, by evil spirits, who are the murderers of souls.
33_interl174: truly: where justice is, there are murderers, because the silver, etc.
33_interl175: the words of divine Scripture turned into the dross of the wicked teaching of the scribes and Pharisees
33_marg82: Silver, etc. Namely, the bright and shining have turned back to vices. Thy silver. Whence: “The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver,” etc.
33_marg83: Dross in Hebrew is sygin, which is the rust of metals, or the refuse and dirt that are burned off by fire.
33_interl176: the sternness of the law with the softness of the Pharisaic tradition, or of heretical perversion
33_marg84: Others: your innkeepers mix the wine with water. Symmachus: thy wine is mixed with water.
33_marg85: Thy wine is mixed with water: because he softens the precepts of holy Scripture, by which he ought to correct his hearers, to suit their will; by mixing in his own sense he corrupts the wine.
33_marg86: Thy wine, etc. Heretics too corrupt the gospel, like the worst tavern-keepers who make water out of wine, when the Lord turned water into wine, which the master of the feast marvelled at; and the queen of Saba, praising in the banquet of Solomon the cupbearers and servants of wine.
33_interl178: the priests who ought to judge the people
33_marg87: Receiving gifts from the scribes and Pharisees, which they took away from the poor. Also in the Lord’s passion they were unbelieving, unwilling to believe in Christ, and companions of thieves: of the scribes and Pharisees, and of Judas the betrayer.
33_marg88: Morally. Companions of thieves. We too ought to beware lest we receive gifts from those who gather riches from the tears of the poor, lest we become companions of thieves, and lest it be said of us: “If thou didst see a thief, thou didst run with him,” etc.
33_interl182: For he does not say they receive gifts but that they love them; for sin lies in the will, not in the thing.
33_marg89: Because they think only those friends who give, whose face they regard not but whose hand they consider. And only those whose purses they drain they judge holy. They give to those from whom they hope for things; they favour them, they extol them or praise their cause.

33_marg196: The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are the seven women. Nor did the Spirit fill him then for the first time, when he appeared upon him in the form of a dove at his baptism, but at the time of his conception.

33_marg300: Go forth to meet, etc. Tropologically. It must be considered that Isaias is commanded to meet the wicked king, rising up from his place, not at the beginning of the conduit but at the farthest ends of the upper pool, which was in the fuller’s field, where filth and stains were cleansed. For although Achaz reigned over Juda, because he was wicked he lingered at the farthest ends of the pool. God therefore has mercy not so much on him as on his people. He calls worldly wisdom and heretical speech the tails of smoking firebrands, whose end is burning. For in vain they have taken counsel to go up against Juda and set over it the son of Tabeel, that is, a good god. For each thinks his own teaching best, but with God’s help their counsel will not stand. But as long as the world stands, it and what belongs to it hold sway within their bounds. But when the end of the world comes, that is, sixty-five years, and both the things of the world which were made in six days and all that pertain to the five senses have reached their end, all things will be dissolved. This the Gentiles and heretics do not believe, and therefore do not understand, according to the Septuagint, as they are called, who say, “With the ear you shall hear.”

How then, in the first year of Achaz, was the prophecy spoken to him of Ezechias who was to be born, when he was already nine years old, unless perhaps they say that the sixth year of the reign of Ezechias, in which Samaria was taken, is called his infancy, not of age but of rule? 33_marg330: Augustine. Of whom it is said: “Before the child know good or evil, he will despise malice.” These two are known in one way and another: good by prudence, and evil by experience. By the prudence of good, evil is known and not felt; for one holds to the good lest evil be felt. By the experience of evil, good is known; for he who has lost it feels how ill it is with him who has lost the good. The child therefore, before he knew by experience the good which he would lack, or the evil which he would feel after losing the good, despised evil that he might choose the good; he likewise was unwilling to lose what he had, or to feel, by losing it, what he ought not to lose.

Therefore the Lord does not rejoice in their young men, because “woe to the city whose king is a child,” and those who have lost God as true Father or Spouse will not obtain mercy. Every heretic is indeed a hypocrite, and whatever he speaks is folly. Therefore the Lord stretches out his hand to punish, and a devouring flame will consume the thorns of their impiety, and their words without virtues (which are compared to an unfruitful thicket) will be wrapped in the smoke of pride. At their punishments the earth will tremble, and the deceived peoples will be handed over to eternal fires or burnings, because for the sake of base gain they spare not even their own, but vie in plundering the deceived, leaving good things, following evil, and are never satisfied with errors; they devour themselves and likewise fight against the Church. Every heretic writes iniquity and deceives the poor, not the rich; whence “the riches of a man are the redemption of his soul.” The poor man does not bear a threat, but the humble is quickly scandalized; and the widow who has lost her husband has lost God, and the orphan who has lost his father, the Creator; whence: “Thou hast forsaken the God that begot thee, and hast forgotten the Lord that created thee.” What then will they do in the day of judgment, when they have deceived so many, and of the calamity coming from afar? To the just man it is said: “The word of God is nigh in thy mouth,” and elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you.” On the other hand, the calamity of the heretics comes from afar and has been prepared for a long time. To whom will they flee for help, since they have a feigned God? To whom will they leave their glory, since all things are pretended? They will not be able to escape the bond with which they have bound very many; they will fall with the several slain, and perish in the death of others. And though they suffer much, and the day of visitation come, there will be no end of their destruction, but they will ever dread the hand of God hanging over them.

33_marg412: The wolf shall dwell, etc. The Jews and our Judaizers contend that at the coming of Christ, whom they await at the end of the world, all the beasts will grow tame. We ask them: if we take everything literally, how shall bodiless things (namely justice and truth) gird the reins of the Lord? and what is worthy of the majesty of the Lord, that the wolf and the lamb should feed together? and the like. But if they answer that these things are said for the future blessedness, that men may enjoy good things in security, let them hear that nothing is good but virtue, and nothing evil but vice. Whence: “Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile”; “turn away from evil, and do good.” But riches and health of bodies and abundance of all things, and their contraries, are called neither good nor evil even among the philosophers. Whence the Stoics, who in most things agree with our teaching, say that nothing is good but honour and virtue alone, nothing evil but baseness.

33_marg534: Nabo: sitting or prophecy. Medaba: from the leap. Esebon: thoughts. Eleale: ascent. Jasa: a deed without command. Segor: small. Luith: cheeks. Oronaim: pit of sorrow. Nemrim: leopards or transgressors. Gallim: calves or heaps of sands. Elym: rams or strong ones. Dibon: sufficient sorrow. Therefore the perverse doctrine, which without the inspiration of God is born in the human sense in the darkness of error, is laid waste by night, and its arguments, that is, its walls, are destroyed by ecclesiastical discourse, and are silent, and are turned to penitence; and over Nabo, that is, prophecy, and sitting, that is, their teachers, and Medaba, where is a barren leap and the dwelling of beasts, there will be howling and lamentation; and from their heads the ornaments of eloquence will be taken away, that they may remain naked and deformed; and if they seemed to have any manliness in the beard, it will be shaved off by the ecclesiastical man and shown to be effeminate and weak. In their crossroads also and the byways of errors, while each one invents what he wishes, he will be girded with the sackcloth of penitence; and upon the housetops, that is, the doctrines in which they believed themselves to be lofty, and in the streets, because they enter the broad way that leadeth to death, there will be howling; neither will they go up into pride, but will go down into weeping. Then they will understand their vain thoughts (which Esebon signifies) and the vain ascent of pride, which Eleale sounds. And their voice will be heard even to the evil works they have done, and the command which they thought to be of God, condemning themselves by their own confession. Therefore the bars, that is, those who were weak in Moab and understood their error, will howl, and will begin to have hope of progress when their soul has howled for itself. Whence the prophet, with the affection of one who suffers with them: “My heart shall cry to Moab.”

And Segor, that is, little penance, if it persevere, will lead them to perfect salvation, which is signified in the heifer of three years. Whence Abraham is commanded to offer a heifer and a ram and a goat of three years, namely a perfect sacrifice, that he may deserve to be the heir of the Lord. But when they have done penance, through Luith, that is, the tears of the cheeks, they ascend to higher things, and as through an opening and entrance of sorrow they will raise the cry of contrition to the Lord, saying: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit: a contrite and humbled heart.” And this will come to pass because the doctrine of the heretics (who are compared to leopards and transgressors) will be desolate. Every herb also and shoot, and whatever seemed green in their speech, has withered, and according to the greatness of their sins they have been visited by God, that him whom they had not perceived through benefits they may know through scourges. Finally they are led to the valley or torrent of willows, that no fruit of the heretics may remain in them. For they say that the nature of the seed of these trees is such that whoever drinks it in a cup becomes childless. Whence the saints: “On the willows in the midst thereof we hung up our instruments” in Babylon. A cry goes round all the borders of the Moabites, of those calling to penance, that through their wailing they may be able to offer the calves of their lips and come to the fountain of the Lord’s rams or of the strong, because Helym signifies both. And the waters of Dibon (which is interpreted sufficient sorrow or grief), which had defiled many by their sprinkling, will be shown to the deceived peoples to have been not for salvation but for blood. Whence the prophetic word promises that over the flowing tears (which is the interpretation of Dibon) they will redouble not one sorrow but many additions of sorrow, that when they have done full penance and fled from Moab they may deserve to have as prince the lion, whom the Septuagint called Ariel, which is interpreted lion of God.

33_marg612: Woe to the land, the winged cymbal. He turns again to Egypt and calls it the cymbal of wings. For the Nile, which, a vast river, the Egeon, coming through Ethiopia and flowing through Egypt, before it was anciently divided here, descending through the mountains with a great noise, was like the sound of many great birds. And therefore the multitude of that people is compared to the sound of wings, swift indeed, and the rushing of the flight of birds is compared to the sound of a cymbal. Or simply, the Nile, very swift, has a sound of wings in the manner of a cymbal. Or a cymbal of wings, because as a bird flies swiftly across, so the Nile swiftly brings forth crops. Or by the cymbal of wings let us understand the help and protection which they promised to those two tribes, according to that: “Protect me under the shadow of thy wings.” Therefore he threatens the Egyptians, because as the Syrians did to the ten tribes, so the Egyptians, by promising help to the Jews, took the fear of the Lord from them.

33_marg624: He will ascend, moreover, by inspiring and by supplying strength in war, that he may strike Egypt, which had led his people astray by promising help. The idols of Egypt were moved, that is, broken by the Assyrians; or perhaps, the Lord working with them, the demons who were in the idols could not give answer to the Egyptians when the Assyrians came upon them. The Lord also ascended upon a light cloud when, having taken a human body not burdened by the corruption of intercourse with a man, he fled into Egypt with Mary and Joseph; and then perhaps the idols of Egypt fell, and the demons in them were struck dumb, and the hearts of the wise men of Egypt melted with fear.

33_marg641: Five cities, etc. Some understand the five books of Moses, which were first translated in Alexandria. But these are better referred to the coming of the Lord. In that day, that is, after the Lord’s passion, there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Chanaan. Egypt, which is sorrow or darkness, is the world, changed into Chanaan. The five cities are the five senses of the body, of which one is of the sun, that is, the eyes, by which we behold the light. Those who serve vices and do not guard the senses of the body from evil pleasures speak the Egyptian language, because they dwell in the darkness of sins; but those who give their effort to virtues speak the language of Chanaan, that is, they speak a changed language, because they are changed from vices to virtues.
33_marg642: The question is asked why the five cities of Egypt speak not the Hebrew language but that of Chanaan. Because, namely, Hebrew means “one who passes over,” who passes from place to place. So as long as we are in the Egypt of this world we cannot speak the Hebrew language, but the language of Chanaan, which is midway between the Hebrew and the Egyptian language and for the most part borders on the Hebrew. Chanaan is interpreted “commotion,” or “as it were answering.” When we depart from Egypt we are moved, and as it were answer the will of the Lord. But because we are still in the world, we cannot speak the Hebrew language.
33_marg643: Those who see a woman to lust after her, and those who hear a judgment of blood, speak the Egyptian tongue. And those who delight in the first ointments, and whose god is the belly, their taste speaks the Egyptian tongue; and so do those who delight in unclean touch.

33_marg647: In that day, etc. Before the coming of the Lord each nation had its own kings, and it was not permitted to pass from one to another, because they feared spies. But the Romans brought all into one, under whom all things were united, and especially after they believed. From the Euphrates to the Tigris was the region of the Assyrians, and those whom the ancients call Assyrians we call Syrians, putting the part for the whole. So after the Lord’s passion the way lay open from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Egyptians pass freely into Assyria, and especially merchants, who run from kingdom to kingdom.
33_marg648: Not that afterwards they were subjugated by them, but because the Roman legions, furnished with Syrian soldiers, guarded Egypt; or because each nation rendered service to the other by exchange of trade. As is read in the book of Machabees, the Assyrians and the Egyptians claimed the kingdom of the Jews for themselves by turns. But at the Lord’s coming it served neither these nor those but the Romans, being of the same condition with them. Whence: “In that day shall Israel be the third,” etc., as if to say: it will not be vexed in turn, standing in the middle between the Assyrians and the Egyptians, but will be the third, serving with them, namely the Romans.

33_marg653: Go and loose, etc. The prophet is commanded to lay aside sackcloth and shoes and to walk naked and barefoot, as a sign to the Egyptians and Ethiopians, who persecuted the people of God. For Egypt is persecuting or afflicting; the Ethiopians are humble and cast down; for he that exalteth himself shall be humbled. These are to be led into captivity for three years, to suffer torments, concerning which: “I had in my mind the eternal years.” Nor let us think the punishments small, but they will be prolonged for great times. And in that very captivity of Egypt, the young men, that is, strengthened in malice, and the old men, who have come to the vices of perfect age, will go naked, that all their crimes may be laid open; for there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed.
33_marg654: And he did so. A wonderful obedience: the most noble man, whose daughter King Manasses took in marriage, as the Hebrews relate, was clothed only in sackcloth; he was not ashamed to go naked, judging nothing more honourable than to obey the Lord.
33_marg655: Barefoot, etc. To be noted: before Azotus is taken, the prophet is clothed in sackcloth with shoes on his feet, that he may lament those who have been wounded by the burning arrows of the devil and serve lust, and that he may be able to tread upon serpents and scorpions, which are in the desert of this world, where there is thirst for all good things. But after Azotus has been taken, as a sign of the captivity of Egypt and Ethiopia, he goes barefoot and naked. For clothed in sackcloth, and with his feet covered with skin, he cannot either stand or walk in the holy land, to which he hastens.

33_marg657: The wonderful providence of God has destroyed all the kingdoms that were proud against one another. Israel hoped, against the will of God, in Damascus and the Syrians, and therefore both were taken captive by the Assyrians. Juda, in the Ethiopians and Egyptians, and these also were conquered by the Assyrians and Chaldeans. The Assyrians, because they presumed on themselves, perished by the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans and Babylonians, lifted up against the Lord, were subjugated by the Medes and Persians, and these by Alexander the Great, who, when he had exalted himself as a god, was killed by poison, and his kingdom was split into parts and afterwards subjugated by the Romans. The Roman empire, which as with iron teeth and claws tore the flesh of the saints, has already for the most part perished. In the end it will perish entirely, when the kingdom of Christ shall have shone forth.

33_marg677: He calleth to me, etc. That is, God, my watchman, calls me day and night to penance, that leaving Seir, which is interpreted bristly and hairy, I may return to dwell with him. Duma is likeness or silence. Idumea is earthly. We can therefore say that, after the likeness of the people of Israel, a multitude of the Gentiles is called, and where before there had been silence of the law of God, there may be the cry of confession. The Church too can relate that the Lord calls to me from Seir, that is, from earthly places, and summons me to salvation, and says to him: O watchman, who rising by night dwellest in the darkness, who art in the flesh without the sin of the flesh, for what cause didst thou will to take a human body? The watchman said: the Samaritan, who carried the wounded man on his own shoulders to the inn. The morning cometh, and the night: to the Gentiles, namely, the sun of justice; to the Jews, darkness; whence: that they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind. Then he speaks to the Gentiles: if you seek me, seek more earnestly.
33_marg678: The morning cometh, etc. As for my people, I will give the light of joy to those returning from captivity; but you I will leave in the night of captivity, because you exulted over the affliction of my people. 33_marg754: After the special rebuke of the single nations, Juda, Babylon, the Philistines, Moab, Damascus, Israel, Egypt, the desert of the sea, Arabia, Idumea, the valley of vision, and Tyre, he describes what the whole world is to suffer at the consummation. Nor does he treat of the nations singly but of all alike. First, what are the torments of the wicked, how heaven and earth shall pass away and sinners be led down into hell; afterwards, how the saints shall be caught up to meet the Lord in the air. So from the special description he passes to the general, which is the fourth rule of Tyconius; for it deals with species and genus, and the person is not changed.

33_marg813: In that day shall visit, etc. The Hebrews hold that the devil (that is, the accuser, which is a Greek name) is called in Hebrew Satan, that is, adversary. Whence it is said: “Satan stood on his right hand to be his adversary”; and he is called Belial, that is, apostate, that is, transgressor, and without yoke. Whence: “What concord hath Christ with Belial?” He is also called by other names; whence: “Upon the asp and the basilisk,” etc. And elsewhere: he who shall take the great whale. Likewise: “Canst thou draw out Leviathan with a hook?” And elsewhere: “This sea dragon which thou hast formed to play therein.” For he was made so that the angels might mock him. Whence: the apostles receive power to tread upon serpents and scorpions. Since, therefore, from that place where the Lord “shall lay waste the earth, and shall strip it,” up to the present chapter, judgment has been foretold against the whole world at the consummation of the world, and the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed, against the devil the final sentence is that the sword be brought upon him.

33_marg816: Leviathan is interpreted as their addition, of whom if not of men? And rightly is he called their addition, since after he brought in the first guilt by evil suggestion, he does not cease daily to increase it by grievous persuasions. For this Leviathan, in that he promised to give himself to man, crept up to him by twisting cords. And while he falsely promises impossible things, he took away true and possible ones. We must ask why, having said serpent, and adding to it crooked, he put the bar in between. Unless perhaps because in the crookedness of the serpent there is slack softness, but in the bar the hardness of rigidity. So that he might mark him as both hard and soft, he names both the bar and the serpent. For he is hard through malice, soft through flattery. He is called a bar who strikes even to death; but a serpent, because he contrives snares and infuses them.

33_marg944: By the ericius is signified the duplicity of an impure mind that defends itself craftily. When the ericius is seized, its head and feet are seen, but once seized it gathers itself into a ball. The head and feet are seen when it is known with what beginning sin came to guilt, or by what steps the guilt was committed. 33_marg946: Morally. Gregory. What is meant by thorns but the pricks of vices? What by nettles but the itchings of sins? In the houses of Babylon thorns and nettles spring up, because in the confusion of a reprobate mind there arise both desires of thoughts, which vex, and sins of works, which prick. The paliurus grows so thick with a surrounding of thorns that for its roughness it can scarcely be touched. Within, the nettle and thorn grow, but both are fenced on the outside by the paliurus; because lesser wicked men do any evil whatever if the greater and most wicked defend it.
33_marg947: Gregory, in the Moralia. Against the perverse mind, under the figure of Judea, it is said: “It shall be the habitation of dragons.” What is meant by dragons but malice? And what is signified by the name of ostrich but hypocrisy? For the ostrich has the appearance of flying, because hypocrisy too offers to all who look an image of holiness, yet knows not the life of holiness. In the perverse mind, then, the dragon lies down and the ostrich is fed, because both the hidden malice is craftily covered and the pretence of goodness is set before the eyes of the beholders. And what is signified by the name of onocentaur but a slippery life, and the proud? For in the Greek tongue onos means ass, and by the name of ass lust is signified. The onocentaurs, therefore, are subject to lust and to vices; thence they lift up the neck. Whence it is well added: “and the hairy ones shall cry out one to another.” Who are figured by the name of the hairy ones, other than those whom the Greeks call planas and the Latins incubi? Their form begins from the human shape but ends in a bestial extremity. By the name of the hairy one, therefore, the roughness of anything whatever is signified, which, even if sometimes begun under pretext of reason, always tends to irrational movements. He ends as a man in a beast when, beginning a fault through an image of reason, he draws it on to an irrational effect. The hairy one cries to the other when malice committed provokes to committing malice.

For they said, “Who can tell if God will turn, and forgive?” Ninive therefore stood. Or was it overthrown? It appears one way to men, another to God. But I see that what the prophet foretold has been fulfilled. Consider what Ninive was, and see that it was overthrown in evil, and built up in good. So it was said to Jeremias: “Behold I will give you to root out, to dig under, and again to build up and to plant.” And hence also comes that saying, “I will strike, and I will heal.”
33_marg984: Since prophecy declares the outcome of things with immovable truth, it seems false that Isaias said to the sick king, “Take order with thy house, for thou shalt die, and not live,” when the Lord added fifteen years to the life of the repenting and praying king. Likewise it is said of Jonas that he preached to the Ninivites, “Yet forty days, and Ninive shall be destroyed,” and yet afterwards, before forty days, the Ninivites obtained the mercy of God. But it must be said that the prophets, reading in that very book of God’s foreknowledge where all things are written, did not perceive all things but some, and in the same manner in which God permitted. For Isaias had read in that book that Ezechias, according to the works he had done, did not deserve a longer life, and according to the nature of the thing could not have it. But he had not read that he would obtain it by tears and prayers. Likewise Jonas had read in the same book that the wickedness of the Ninivites, according to what they were doing, was to be fulfilled on the fortieth day, and so their city to be destroyed. But he had not read that through his warning they would do penance and so obtain mercy. Each therefore preached what he had read, and as far as concerned them the truth was unchangeable, because they intended to deceive no one. For Augustine says: whoever believes as he speaks, even if he does not speak what is true, yet speaks faithfully. For the Lord, as Gregory says, changes the sentence but not the counsel. By sentence we ought to understand the sense of the words; the counsel, however, is from the eternal ordering. God had revealed the sentence to his servants, but not the counsel, so that by their threats he might strike repentance into his people and so have mercy on them. It seems, however, that they did not read in the book of life the words which they spoke. For since Isaias said simply “thou shalt die, and not live,” and Jonas “Ninive shall be destroyed,” and these things were not to come to pass, those things which were not to be do not seem to be in the book of God. But it must be known that God considers some things in two ways: according to merits and according to the nature of the thing, which are said to be inferior causes, and according to his own counsel. Whence God had foreseen that Ezechias would die, according to merit or according to nature, though it was not to be, and that he would not die, according to his own counsel. Both therefore were written in the book of life, but the one he permitted his prophet to read, the other was not permitted. He spoke the truth and was not deceived, because he read so; nor did he lie, because he so believed; and he spoke according to those inferior causes, although simply and without addition. If someone saw a blind man and said, “this man will see no more,” even if by divine counsel he received light, he would not be lying, because he followed the nature of the thing. In the same way Jonas also saw the overthrow of the Ninivites in the divine mind, which yet was not to be, because what he saw, he saw according to their merits. But that they were converted was of the counsel of God, which he did not see.

They say also that he is a brazier, a smith, who forged Abraham, and with the hammer of his art brought him forth to better things, and said: It is good that thou be joined fast to the fear of the Lord and united to him; and he strengthened him with the nails of the precepts, that he might remain in the fear of the Lord.

33_marg1141: To my anointed Cyrus, etc. Allegorically. We can say this of an ecclesiastical man to whom God gives speech and wisdom, that by his disputation he may overthrow opposing sects, as with Stephen, whose wisdom his enemies could not resist; and that he may subject to his power the kings, that is, the patriarchs of the several heresies, and open and break open what by the art of dialectic seemed shut up, and bring into the open the secrets of the heretics, overcoming and convincing them; or that he may know the secrets of Christ, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” God calls such a man by name because he is the defender of his servant Jacob and of his elect Israel. Him he takes up and likens to his own word; which everyone ought to beware of, lest he think that what he speaks is his own, lest he deserve to hear: “I girded thee, and thou hast not known me.” For when he has taught all that there is no other God but the one God of Jacob and Israel, Marcion will be confounded, who understands two gods: one good, the other unjust; one the maker of visible things, the other of invisible. Of whom the first makes light, the second darkness; the former peace, the latter evil; whereas one and the same God has made both according to the difference of merits.

33_marg1186: Gregory. Come down, sit in the dust, O daughter of Babylon. In this place the human mind is called a virgin, not as uncorrupted (as I think) but as unfruitful. And because Babylon means confusion, the unfruitful mind is rightly called the daughter of Babylon, which, in that it brings forth no good works (since it is not ordered by any rule of right living), is begotten as it were of its mother, confusion. But if she is called a virgin not as unfruitful but as corrupted, after she has lost the state of salvation, then what was said, “come down,” is spoken to heap up her confusion. For the human mind stands on high when it longs for heavenly rewards. But it comes down from this state when, shamefully bound, it submits itself to the fleeting desires of the world; to which it is fittingly added at once: Sit in the dust. For one who comes down sits in the dust, because, forsaking heavenly things, sprinkled with earthly thoughts, he grows vile among the lowest things. Sit on the ground, because you were unwilling to raise yourself from heavenly conversation, to humble yourself prostrate beneath yourself among earthly things. Whence it is necessarily added: There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans. Chaldeans are interpreted as fierce; and they are very fierce who, following their own pleasures, do not know how to spare even their own impulses. But the daughter of the fierce has no throne, because the mind that is born from wicked desires to the love of the world, and is darkened in them, in that it submits itself to earthly desires loses its seat, and as it were is driven from the session of its judge, since it wanders through outward lusts; and often by just judgment it is left to its own will, and under the things it anxiously seeks the toilsome services of the world are relaxed. For thou shalt no more be called delicate and tender. It is certain that parents spare their tender daughters and do not afflict them with hard and servile works. Almighty God therefore calls a soul as it were a tender daughter when he calls back each one’s beloved soul from the toilsome servitudes of this world, lest while it is affected by outward things it be hardened by inward desires. But the daughter of the Chaldeans is not called delicate and tender, because the mind given to wicked desires is left to the labor of this age, so that outwardly it serves the world like a handmaid, because inwardly it does not love God as a daughter. Whence also she is said to take the millstone and grind meal. The mill is turned in a circle and meal is brought forth. Every action of this world is evil, which while it heaps up many cares turns human minds as it were in a circle, and casts out from itself as it were meal, because the seduced heart always begets the most minute thoughts. Sometimes, however, one who in quiet was believed to be of some importance is laid bare when set in any action. Be uncovered, etc. For the baseness is laid bare by the empty performance of work, when a mind vile and abject is recognized in the display of action, which in quiet was before thought great. The mind uncovers the shoulder when it shows its work, which was unknown; it reveals the leg when it makes known that by certain steps of desires it gapes after the gains of the world. She also crosses the rivers when she ceaselessly seeks the actions of this age, which daily flow away to their end. And while she leaves some and follows others, she passes as it were from river to river.

33_marg1309: Jerome. The Septuagint: I will give thee a carbuncle, etc. The carbuncle is the fiery word, which, the darkness of errors being put to flight, enlightens the hearts of believers. This is that by which the lips of Isaias are purged, and according to Genesis it is born in the land of Evilath. The sapphire has the likeness of heaven, signifying those who say with Socrates: I climb the air and look down on the sun, and with Paul: “our conversation is in heaven.” The jasper fortifies the bulwarks of those who can destroy every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God and subject falsehood to truth. There are many kinds of jasper: one is like the emerald, which is found in the springs of Thermodon and is called amastisios, by which they think all phantoms are put to flight. Another is greener than the sea and tinted as if with flowers, which is found in Phrygia on Ida, in the deepest places, a mirror. Another is found near the Hiberians and Hyrcanians and the Caspian Sea, and especially the lake Neusis. Another is like snow and sea foam, reddish with a gently mingled colour. We have said these things so that we may recognize all the spiritual graces in the bulwarks of the Church, by which vain fears are put to flight; and he who has them says: “my cousin, the beloved, is white and ruddy.”

Whence also they say to the angels accompanying the Lord: Who is this that cometh from Edom? And David likewise: “Who is this King of Glory?” Yet Augustine seems to say on Genesis that all the angels, from their very creation, at once knew in the contemplation of their creator whatever he was to do. Esau means oaken or strong as oak. Seir, rough, that is, hairy. Here, however, according to the interpretation, it signifies not the man himself but the world. So also Bosra, that is, fortified or strong, signifies here not its own thing but, according to its interpretation, hell, where the souls were held firmly as if under many guards; whence: “Who will bring me into the strong city?” Or the earthly Jerusalem, which was fortified with very strong walls, in which the Lord suffered. Whence Homer, according to Josephus, Jerome says, from whom Jerusalem is interpreted fortified or strong. Bosra, however, is a city situated neither in the promised land nor in Edom but in Moab. Therefore Christ came from the bloody world; “he came from Bosra with dyed garments,” that is, with bodily members, from the fortified city, namely Jerusalem, where he suffered. 33_marg1518: Abraham knew us not, etc. Abraham was called from the Gentiles to the faith, and according to the quality of his former and later condition he obtained a change of name. Jacob also acquired, with much labour, to be called Israel; whence Abraham had three wives, Jacob four. Isaac kept his old name to the end, and, signifying the chastity of the Church, was content with one wife. These, therefore, who pray out of worse things, take on the likeness of a change to a better state of those to whom joys succeeded after sorrows. And this is what they ask: that he who is their father may not forget his sons, lest through them the name of God be blasphemed among the Gentiles.

33_marg1599: As, etc. Almighty God, as merciful and compassionate, compares himself now to an eagle, now to a hen, now to a caressing mother, that he may at least win you over with caresses. As also the eagle makes her nest on inaccessible rocks, that access may be open to no one; and in the middle she places an amethyst stone, which, according to the naturalists, drives away all poisons, to keep off serpents, and certain other secrets of nature. So he himself in our hearts places a stone, that is, his faith, namely himself, who is the stone cut out without hands from the mountain, by which all the poisons of the devil are driven away. By the month, therefore, is understood the moon; by the moon, which now waxes, now wanes, and, as the naturalists and philosophers say, receives from the sun the light it does not have, the Church is understood, of whom it is said: “He shall continue with the sun, and before the moon,” and elsewhere: “Fair as the moon, bright as the sun”; and this is “month after month.”
